title: Fabrinet Reports Tonight. The AI Optics Trade Needs One More Beat.
subtitle: Fabrinet heads into its fiscal Q4 print Monday with record momentum: a 39%-growth quarter already banked, Lumentum's blowout read-through behind it, and the Street expecting roughly $1.28 billion in revenue. Here's what actually matters tonight.
summary: Fabrinet reports fiscal Q4 and full-year 2026 results after the close Monday, Aug 17. The March quarter is already on the books — record revenue of $1.214 billion, up 39% year over year, and non-GAAP EPS of $3.72. Tonight's consensus estimates call for roughly $1.28 billion in revenue (up about 41% YoY) and EPS in the $3.81–$3.85 range, with the company's own guidance at $1.25–$1.29 billion and $3.72–$3.87. With Lumentum's AI-optics quarter doubling year over year, reports of an FCC ban on Chinese optical transceivers, and shares climbing nearly 9% into the print, here's what matters when the numbers drop.

bodyHtml:
Fabrinet reports fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close on Monday, and the market has already decided what it wants to hear: more of the same. Shares climbed roughly nine percent in a single session last Wednesday, riding an optics rally that carried the stock sharply higher into the print, and the sector has been levitating ever since. The AI optical-packaging leader has spent the past year turning guidance into beat after beat, and tonight's numbers are expected to extend the streak. The catch is that the bar has never been higher.

The Numbers That Matter
Price LIVE$570.22
Market Cap$20.4B
Forward P/E~34x
Total Revenue (TTM)$4.24B
52-Week Low$272.49
52-Week High$748.89
Analyst ConsensusModerate Buy
Analyst Target Mean—
Price refreshes live · All other figures as of August 14, 2026

Start with the quarter already on the books, because it sets the tone. When Fabrinet reported fiscal Q3 in early May, revenue hit a record $1.214 billion, up 39 percent year over year and comfortably above the Street's $1.19 billion, while non-GAAP EPS of $3.72 beat consensus by fourteen cents. Data Center Interconnect revenue nearly doubled to $197 million, telecom optical rose 55 percent, and the high-performance compute segment added $107 million, up 25 percent sequentially. The one wrinkle: the company shipped less datacom than customers wanted because lasers, memory, and ASICs were in short supply. Demand exceeding supply is the best problem a contract manufacturer can have.

Tonight's print is expected to look similar — and note the word expected, because these are consensus estimates, not reported results. Analysts are looking for roughly $1.28 billion of revenue, up about 41 percent year over year, and non-GAAP EPS in the $3.81 to $3.85 range. Management's own guidance from May pointed to $1.25 billion to $1.29 billion of revenue and EPS of $3.72 to $3.87, so the Street is camped near the top of the range. The full-year estimates are just as demanding: consensus EPS of $13.81 for fiscal 2026 and $17.32 for fiscal 2027, with revenue on track to top $4.6 billion for the year.

The tailwinds are fresh and concrete. Lumentum, the closest optics bellwether, reported its first billion-dollar quarter on August 11 with revenue up 109 percent year over year, and management flagged the shift to 800G and 1.6T cloud modules with co-packaged optics laser orders outrunning supply. Fabrinet shares rallied on that read-through, and the optics complex has been bid up ever since. When the closest comparable company blows out and guides higher, the market assumes the contract manufacturer feeding it does too.

Then there is geopolitics. Reports from early August say the FCC is drafting a ban on imports of new Chinese optical transceiver modules on national security grounds, with publication possible before year-end. Chinese suppliers dominate roughly two-thirds of global transceiver units, so any meaningful restriction would push hyperscalers toward non-Chinese manufacturers — Fabrinet, Coherent, Lumentum, and Applied Optoelectronics are the only major options at scale. The caveat is that Western capacity cannot replace Chinese volume overnight, and the rule could still be shelved. Even as a scenario, it is a structural tailwind for the largest non-China optical manufacturer.

The deeper story is the ramp Fabrinet is quietly executing. The company qualified two 800G scale-out transceiver programs with a hyperscale customer and began shipping them in the June quarter, with volumes set to climb through fiscal 2027. NVIDIA remains the anchor customer at roughly 28 percent of revenue, and transceivers make up about 60 percent of networking cost inside AI clusters, so optical content scales with every GPU deployed. Roughly $940 million of net cash and essentially zero debt fund the Thailand capacity buildout without breaking a sweat.

None of this is free. The stock has already rallied hard into the print, which means a beat-and-raise is substantially priced in — anything short of fiscal 2027 guidance that tops the Street could sting. Supply constraints that capped datacom growth in the March quarter may linger into the next ramp. And concentration is real: NVIDIA and Cisco anchor the customer base — NVIDIA alone is roughly 28 percent of revenue — and the top four customers together account for well over half, so order timing at the biggest names moves the whole company.

The honest read is that Fabrinet is the cleanest pure-play on the AI optics supercycle, and tonight's print will likely confirm the story rather than break it. The risk sits less in the quarter than in the valuation, with shares up roughly 75 percent over the past year. Watch three things on the call: fiscal 2027 guidance, the pace of the hyperscale transceiver ramp, and any commentary on component supply. If management threads those needles, the optics trade keeps its leader.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in FN. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
